title: Breaking the Chain: Agent Continuations for Resumable AI Workflows - Greg Benson

primary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 93%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary object is agent loops, multi-level agent architecture, and a control-plane continuation mechanism for suspending and resuming agents. The continuation mechanism is a developer-facing protocol and Python tool aimed at software builders integrating resumable agents into existing frameworks. A working Python prototype with a live demo exists on GitHub but is not yet integrated into production agent frameworks. Prerequisites are basic understanding of AI agents, LLM tool calling, and Python, targeting intermediate practitioners. Conference-style presentation with code walkthroughs and a live multi-level agent demo. All supporting evidence is drawn from statements made directly in the transcript.

summary: Greg Benson (University of San Francisco professor and SnapLogic Chief Scientist) introduces agent continuations, developed at SnapLogic's Agent Creator research group. The talk addresses two core production challenges: human-in-the-loop approval for high-risk tool calls (e.g., transferring money, deleting accounts) and state preservation for long-running agents vulnerable to network or hardware failures. Current agent frameworks typically require the agent loop to persist continuously—even when waiting for human responses—which is problematic for distributed deployments. Agent continuations, inspired by programming language continuation theory, enable capturing an agent's complete execution state at any point and resuming execution later. The messages array already maintained in LLM interactions provides much of the needed state; the continuation object wraps this with additional metadata including a resume request (indicating which tool call to resume at) and a processed field (indicating approval status). Key to the design is that once suspended, no agent loops need remain running—all state is captured for restart. The continuation format is recursive, handling arbitrary depths of nesting for multi-level agents where orchestrator agents call sub-agents. A live demonstration shows a two-level HR agent with an email tool and an account agent sub-agent; the sub-agent's authorize account tool requires approval, causing suspension. The continuation object propagates upward through agent levels, accumulating state at each level. The application layer inspects extracted metadata, updates the approval, and resends the continuation via the same request method. Upon resumption, the framework reconstructs all agent and sub-agent state; the final result contains a normal messages array with no continuation artifacts. The Python prototype is built on the OpenAI Python API with no other dependencies and is available on GitHub. Future work includes more general suspension points (time-based, turn-count-based, asynchronous) and extending existing frameworks like Strands or Pydantic AI rather than building a separate framework. The approach is novel in combining human approval with arbitrary nesting depth, which other frameworks' state management solutions lack. Continuations were also prototyped in SnapLogic's Agent Creator visual platform.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Greg Benson introduces himself and the concept of agent continuations developed at SnapLogic. He outlines the core challenges: human approval during agent processing, long-running agents in the presence of failure, and distributed execution considerations.

sections.title: Agent Challenges and Basic Execution
sections.summary: Detailed look at challenges including human-in-the-loop for high-risk tasks, long-running agent failure susceptibility, and distributed environment considerations. Basic agent execution is described as a loop of LLM calls and tool calls, with tools potentially being sub-agents themselves.

sections.title: Execution Scenarios and Multi-level Agents
sections.summary: Three key execution scenarios: tool calls requiring human approval, rate limiting from LLM APIs, and long-running agents needing failure tolerance. Discussion of increasingly sophisticated multi-level agent architectures with orchestrator agents calling sub-agents, raising the question of how to handle approval and state saving in these configurations.

sections.title: Agent Loop Persistence
sections.summary: Introduces the concept of agent loop persistence: most current frameworks require the agent loop to run continuously, even when waiting for human input. The goal is to develop a mechanism allowing full shutdown and restart of agent loops when resumption is needed.

sections.title: Agent Continuations Concept and Messages Array Insight
sections.summary: Agent continuations are inspired by programming language continuation theory, enabling snapshot-and-resume at any execution point. Key insight: the messages array already logs interaction history replayed to the LLM for each inference, providing much of the needed state for continuations, though not quite sufficient alone.

sections.title: Framework Usage with Continuations
sections.summary: Walkthrough of framework usage: standard approach uses tool decorators and agent class; continuation approach adds approval-designated tools and ContinuationAgent class. When an agent suspends, it returns a continuation object with metadata. The application updates the continuation and resends it via the same request method to resume.

sections.title: Continuation Object Structure and Recursive Nesting
sections.summary: Details the continuation object structure: it wraps the standard messages array with metadata including a resume request (indicating which tool call to resume at) and a processed field (approval status). The format is recursive, handling arbitrary nesting depths for multi-level agents, where sub-agent continuations contain their own messages, resume requests, and processed fields. Key point: once suspended, no agent loops need remain running.

sections.title: Multi-level HR Agent Example and Continuation Propagation
sections.summary: Full example of a multi-level HR agent with an email tool and an account agent sub-agent (with create account and authorize account tools, the latter requiring approval). Diagram shows how the continuation object propagates upward through agent levels, accumulating state at each level, until the application layer receives the full object for inspection and action.

sections.title: Live Demo: Suspension, Approval, and Resumption
sections.summary: Live demo sends a prompt to create a new account; the agent suspends when authorize account needs approval. The response object contains the continuation with top-level messages, sub-agent messages, and an approval object. After manual approval update, the edited continuation is sent back; the agent reconstructs state and completes successfully. Final result is a normal messages array with no continuation artifacts.

sections.title: Implementation Details, Future Work, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Prototype built on OpenAI Python API with no other dependencies; available on GitHub. Future work includes general suspension points (time, turns, async) and extending existing frameworks like Strands or Pydantic AI rather than building a separate one. The approach is novel in combining human approval with arbitrary nesting depth. Also prototyped in SnapLogic Agent Creator visual platform. Links: GitHub repo and agentcreator.com.
